The move confirms Justin Fields is out of the Jets' plans.
Geno Smith|QB.strength: The Seattle baseline is a real NFL starter — 68.5% completions at 7.4 Y/A with 76 TD to 36 INT across 54 games. The 2026 skill group is loaded: Garrett Wilson, Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell, rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq.
Geno Smith|QB.weakness: A disastrous walk year in Las Vegas — a league-leading 17 INT, a career-high 55 sacks, QB27 in fantasy PPG with two usable weeks all season. PFF had him 4th-lowest in passer rating under pressure but 19th from a clean pocket, which is the whole story in two numbers.

Jacoby Brissett|QB.role: Week 1 starter, confirmed by first-year HC Mike LaFleur, on a reworked one-year $15.5M deal agreed Jul 26, 2026. Took over for the final 12 games of 2025 after Kyler Murray's season-ending foot injury and went 1-11 as a starter while averaging 40.3 attempts per game — Arizona led the NFL in pass attempts during his starts. Murray is gone (released, now Minnesota's starter); third-round rookie Carson Beck and Gardner Minshew sit behind Brissett.
Jacoby Brissett|QB.strength: Volume is the whole thesis — 288 pass yards per start and 23 TD to 8 INT over 12 starts in 2025. The weapons are genuinely good: Marvin Harrison Jr., Trey McBride and Michael Wilson, who just signed a 3yr/$75M extension.
Jacoby Brissett|QB.weakness: 1-11 as a starter. FantasyPros expects the league-leading pass volume to regress. Arizona drafted Beck specifically as succession, and the same analysis flags a real chance Beck gets an audition during the season.

Braelon Allen|RB.role: Clear 1B behind Breece Hall entering year three. Took first-team reps through the second half of camp while Hall was out with a groin injury and started the Aug 21 preseason win over Pittsburgh with the starters. Hall is expected back for the Week 1 opener at Tennessee and will get the lion's share; Isaiah Davis (knee) could push Allen for the No. 2 job once healthy.
Braelon Allen|RB.strength: Strong preseason — 7 carries for 48 yards (6.86 YPC) and a TD including a 31-yard score against Tampa Bay. Power profile at 6'1"/235 with 26 bench reps at the combine, second among backs, which is the short-yardage and goal-line archetype. 3,494 rushing yards and 35 TD at Wisconsin.
Braelon Allen|RB.weakness: No passing-game role to speak of — one catch for five yards all preseason. Minimal 2025 usage before a Week 4 season-ending knee injury (18 carries, 76 yards). The backup job itself is not locked; CBS flags Davis as a threat once cleared.

Emmett Johnson|RB.role: Fifth-round rookie (No. 161, Nebraska, via a trade with Pittsburgh), signed May 4, 2026. Opened as RB3 behind Kenneth Walker III and Emari Demercado. Camp went badly — Andy Reid publicly flagged his pad level in early August and 2025 seventh-rounder Brashard Smith took first-team goal-line reps instead. Kansas City then waived Demercado at cutdowns, which reads as clearing a path to RB2, though that specific depth-chart conclusion rests on aggregated reporting rather than a dated beat article.
Emmett Johnson|RB.strength: A genuine college statistical outlier — 251 carries for 1,451 yards and 12 TD plus 46 catches for 370 yards in his final Nebraska season, the only FBS player to average 150+ scrimmage yards per game that year. The pass-catching profile is the complement Walker's between-the-tackles game lacks.
Emmett Johnson|RB.weakness: Publicly criticised on fundamentals by his own head coach in camp. Lost early goal-line work to Brashard Smith. Rookie fifth-rounder with no path to volume unless Walker misses time.

Kimani Vidal|RB.role: Entrenched backup to Omarion Hampton, competing with Keaton Mitchell for change-of-pace and passing-down snaps. Played 14 snaps with 5 carries in the preseason opener against Houston. Re-signed as an exclusive rights free agent and viewed as a roster lock at worst as RB3.
Kimani Vidal|RB.strength: Has already done the job — 643 rushing yards and 3 TD plus 16 catches for 136 yards and a TD across 13 games (10 starts) in 2025 stepping in for an injured Hampton. Entering year three with a tenure edge over the other backups in a new scheme.
Kimani Vidal|RB.weakness: The 2025 production was volume, not efficiency — among 49 qualifying backs he was 30th in explosive run rate, 34th in missed-tackle rate and 36th in yards after contact per attempt. FantasyPros labels him "a late-round handcuff option only."

MarShawn Lloyd|RB.role: Presumed Week 1 lead back after Josh Jacobs was placed on the Commissioner's Exempt List around Aug 30-31, 2026 on two misdemeanor charges with an initial court date of Nov 17. Critically, this is not team-announced. Packers.com (Sep 2) notes Lloyd has six carries and one reception total as a pro entering year three yet is "quite likely" the Week 1 feature back. Kaleb Johnson, traded in from Pittsburgh on Aug 30, and third-down back Chris Brooks sit behind him.
MarShawn Lloyd|RB.strength: Testable athleticism at 5'9"/220 — 4.46 forty, 36" vertical, 118" broad. Top-20 in yards after contact per attempt in his final two college seasons, with 7.1 YPC and 13 catches in his last USC year. GM Brian Gutekunst called him "as ready as he's ever been."
MarShawn Lloyd|RB.weakness: Roughly ten offensive NFL snaps across two seasons; missed all of 2025 with a recurring hamstring traced to a 2020 ACL. Exceeded 15 carries in a game only three times in his entire college career. Modest preseason usage (10 carries, 30 yards).

Mike Washington Jr.|RB.role: Fourth-round rookie (No. 122, Arkansas) who has run with the first team since Ashton Jeanty sprained his right ankle in practice around Aug 30. HC Klint Kubiak said on Sep 4 that Jeanty is "on the mend" and is optimistic but has not confirmed him for the Week 1 opener; if Jeanty sits, the Review-Journal has Washington "poised to bear the brunt of the workload."
Mike Washington Jr.|RB.strength: Rare size-speed at 6'2"/223 — a 4.33 forty with a 1.51 ten-yard split, fastest among 2026 combine backs, plus a 39" vertical. Preseason production backed it up: 168 yards on 23 carries (7.3 YPC) across three games including a 53-yarder. Real college volume — 587 career attempts, and 1,070 yards at 6.4 YPC in his final Arkansas season.
Mike Washington Jr.|RB.weakness: Only one season at a Power Four school. Passing-game role is unproven and undiscussed publicly. Behind a healthy Jeanty he is a pure contingency asset.

Nicholas Singleton|RB.role: Fifth-round rookie, No. 165 overall, acquired via a trade with Buffalo (confirmed on the Titans' own player page). Depth-chart standing is genuinely unsettled — FantasyPros' dynasty analyst has him starting as RB4 while the Aug 10 unofficial depth-chart recap listed him sixth among running backs. Tony Pollard is the clear lead with Tyjae Spears second in the pass-game pecking order; Michael Carter, Julius Chestnut and Kalel Mullings are competing for the same roster spot, which beat writer Jim Wyatt says will come down to special-teams value.
Nicholas Singleton|RB.strength: Penn State's all-time leader with 55 career TD, 45 of them rushing, plus 5,586 all-purpose yards, and 12+ rushing TD in three of four seasons. Pass protection translates — 3 sacks and 10 hurries allowed on 173 college pass-block snaps. 6'0"/219 fits a between-the-tackles and check-down role.
Nicholas Singleton|RB.weakness: Scouting notes flag tentative vision at the line, choppy footwork in space and limited change of direction. Missed back-to-back practices in mid-August with no stated cause. Buried behind two established veterans with no first-month path to touches.

Ray Davis|RB.role: Clear backup to James Cook III with Ty Johnson also in the room. No standalone role projected absent a Cook injury.
Ray Davis|RB.strength: Efficient with the work he gets — 4.7 yards per carry in 2025. Reliable hands: 27 receptions on 32 career targets. Strong scoring rate at 8 total TD on 198 career touches.
Ray Davis|RB.weakness: Zero standalone value in a Cook-centric offense. Cook has missed two games in his entire career, so the injury scenario that unlocks Davis rarely arrives. Josh Allen's goal-line rushing further caps the TD equity that would otherwise flow to a backup.

Sean Tucker|RB.role: RB3 behind Bucky Irving and offseason addition Kenny Gainwell, who are expected to work as a 1A-1B. Signed a new one-year, $2.5M fully guaranteed deal around Aug 30, 2026, replacing his prior $3.52M restricted tender.
Sean Tucker|RB.strength: The snap trend is up — a career-high 177 offensive snaps in 2025. Real scoring production when given the ball: 8 total TD in 2025 including a 3-TD, 19-carry, 106-yard game against Buffalo. Pewter Report says he would be a primary backup or starter-competitor on other rosters.
Sean Tucker|RB.weakness: Third on the depth chart behind an explicit 1A-1B plan. FantasyPros projects 39.3 carries and 1.5 catches for the entire season. No identified pass-game carve-out of his own.

Chris Bell|WR.role: Third-round rookie, No. 94 overall out of Louisville. Confirmed on Miami's initial 53-man roster announced Aug 30, 2026 as one of seven receivers — Jalen Tolbert, Malik Washington, Caleb Douglas, Bell, Kevin Coleman Jr., Ryan Miller, AJ Henning. Opened camp on Active/NFI recovering from an ACL tear in his final Louisville season and was activated on Aug 17, 2026. Reported to be trending toward playing in Week 1.
Chris Bell|WR.strength: Strong final college season — 72 receptions for 917 yards and 6 TD in 11 games, with a 41.2% dominator rating that ranked third in his draft class. Size and speed at 6'2"/222 with in-pads GPS tracking reported in the low 4.3s.
Chris Bell|WR.weakness: Coming off an ACL tear with a real practice-reps deficit against healthy rookies and incumbents. Entering an unsettled QB situation rather than a clean passing environment. Analysts frame him as a better dynasty investment than an immediate redraft target.

Cooper Kupp|WR.role: Seattle's post-cutdown depth chart (Aug 31, 2026) lists him specifically as the slot receiver, with Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Montorie Foster Jr. at one outside spot and Rashid Shaheed and Tory Horton at the other. That is a deliberate formation change from 2025, when Kupp and Smith-Njigba overlapped heavily in the slot. He projects as the No. 3 target behind Smith-Njigba and Shaheed.
Cooper Kupp|WR.strength: Still drew real volume in a diminished role — 47 catches for 593 yards and 2 TD on 70 targets across 16 games in 2025. Historically a high target-rate earner even as a secondary option (24.2% target rate per route in 2024 alongside Puka Nacua). Seahawks officials have called him a force multiplier entering his tenth season.
Cooper Kupp|WR.weakness: The athletic decline is measured, not impressionistic. ESPN tracking has his openness rank falling from 15th of 160 receivers in 2021 to 141st of 159 in 2024, with YAC per reception dropping from 5.8 to a career-low 4.0 over the same span. Targets cratered on arrival in Seattle — 8.3 per game with the Rams in 2024 down to 4.4 per game in 2025.

De'Zhaun Stribling|WR.role: Second-round rookie (No. 33, Ole Miss) who entered a room with Mike Evans locked in outside and was ticketed to compete with Ricky Pearsall and Christian Kirk for the No. 2/3 job. Pearsall's season-ending PCL injury removed one competitor outright. Caught 11 of 13 targets for 109 yards across the first two preseason games — what PFN called a "loud preseason."
De'Zhaun Stribling|WR.strength: The preseason target-conversion rate is the cleanest signal available on a rookie. PFN reports the front office graded him well above public consensus, and his summer reinforced that internal grade. Lands in a Kyle Shanahan offense with Brock Purdy — one of the league's more efficient passing environments.
De'Zhaun Stribling|WR.weakness: Not a plug-and-play Week 1 starter; Footballguys puts the realistic timeline at the first quarter of the season. A camp hamstring interrupted his momentum. Footballguys also flags him as one of the widest range-of-outcome rookie WRs in the class — the same analysis that likes him allows he could be a non-factor.

Dontayvion Wicks|WR.role: Green Bay traded him to Philadelphia on Apr 13, 2026 for a 2026 fifth and a 2027 sixth (Packers.com). He sits WR2 on the Eagles' depth chart behind DeVonta Smith and ahead of rookie Makai Lemon, with Hollywood Brown and Elijah Moore behind. The role got materially bigger when Philadelphia traded A.J. Brown to New England in June 2026.
Dontayvion Wicks|WR.strength: Three-year Green Bay production of 108 receptions, 1,328 yards and 11 TD across 46 games. Howie Roseman called him "a physical, explosive player at the top of routes," and Nick Sirianni compared his release and route-running to Keenan Allen; CB Quinyon Mitchell called him one of the most underrated players he has faced.
Dontayvion Wicks|WR.weakness: His most recent season was modest — 30/332/2 in 2025 as a WR3/4. Still learning the offense as of July ("we're all still learning... it's just details"). Sits behind DeVonta Smith rather than being the focal point.

Isaac TeSlaa|WR.role: Uncontested WR3 behind Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams. Confirmed: Detroit kept only four receivers on the initial 53-man roster set Aug 30, 2026 — St. Brown, Williams, TeSlaa and Tay Martin — releasing veteran Greg Dortch outright. Fifth-round rookie Kendrick Law tore his ACL in a non-contact OTA drill in early June 2026 and went to season-ending IR, removing him from the competition entirely.
Isaac TeSlaa|WR.strength: Size-speed profile at 6'4"/216 with a 4.43 forty. Flashed as a rookie in 2025 — 16 catches for 239 yards and 6 TD after Detroit traded Tim Patrick to Jacksonville and opened the WR3 job. Receivers coach Scottie Montgomery said the team is "not too concerned" about the quiet 2026 camp, noting he was deliberately matched against the opponent's top corners.
Isaac TeSlaa|WR.weakness: Empty preseason opener — 0 for 3 with an interception on the first ball thrown his way. Beat writer Dave Birkett called the camp "bland." Route running was the knock coming out of Arkansas, lacking the quickness to separate against tight press. Limited college volume.

Ja'Kobi Lane|WR.role: Third-round rookie, No. 80 overall out of USC. Listed second-team on Baltimore's first unofficial depth chart behind Rashod Bateman and Zay Flowers, but has run with the first team through camp. Started the first preseason game and played into the second quarter, played a reduced role in game two, and sat game three entirely — a pattern beat writers read as the team protecting a settled WR3 rather than a bubble player. Flowers and Bateman both sat the whole preseason.
Ja'Kobi Lane|WR.strength: Outstanding ball skills, body control and contested-catch ability, with reportedly the largest hands in the rookie class — a genuine red-zone and fade-route weapon out of USC. Lamar Jackson publicly compared him to a combination of Odell Beckham Jr. and DeAndre Hopkins, which is a meaningful trust signal from the man throwing the ball.
Ja'Kobi Lane|WR.weakness: Route-running is unrefined — glides through the stem, inconsistent attacking leverage, came from a scheme that did not ask for a pro route tree. Dropped four passes in each of his last two college seasons against 92 catches. Limited separation and a modest YAC threat; slender frame can be outmuscled in press.

Jalen Nailor|WR.role: Signed a 3-year, $35M deal with $23M guaranteed in unrestricted free agency on Mar 9, 2026, ending four years in Minnesota. Raiders Wire (Aug 14) has him expected to occupy the No. 1 receiver role and describes him as the most productive pass-catcher in team drills behind only Brock Bowers. Competes with Tre Tucker, Jack Bech and Donte Thornton Jr.
Jalen Nailor|WR.strength: Career-high 2025 with Minnesota — 29 catches for 444 yards at 15.4 per catch and 4 TD, in a part-time No. 3 role. Red-zone and vertical scoring history: 6 TD on 28 catches in 2023. The contract is the front office stating what it thinks his role is.
Jalen Nailor|WR.weakness: Career volume is genuinely thin — 69 catches for 1,066 yards over four seasons and 55 games, never topping 29 catches. Unproven as a lead target; his 2025 role was a distant third behind Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. Sixth-round pedigree with 12 catches total across his first two seasons.

Jaylin Noel|WR.role: Listed as Houston's Week 1 slot receiver on the Texans' Sep 2 post-cuts depth chart — X Nico Collins, Z Xavier Hutchinson, slot Noel — with Kayshon Boutte and Jared Wayne behind. In his 2025 rookie year, 65.9% of his routes came from the slot, 25th among receivers with 30+ slot targets. Christian Kirk's departure opened the job.
Jaylin Noel|WR.strength: Real slot role and route fit established as a rookie third-round pick out of Iowa State. Positive spring and preseason reviews reportedly earned him increased passing-game usage. Two receivers above him on the roster — Jayden Higgins and Tank Dell — are on injured reserve, thinning the room.
Jaylin Noel|WR.weakness: The Boutte trade directly caps his snaps: RotoBaller reads it as an "almost certainty" that Noel is off the field in two-receiver sets, since Boutte plays opposite Collins in those packages. Projected for roughly 23 catches, 265 yards and 2 TD on 47 targets. Carries a Questionable designation on RotoWire's current depth chart with no specified injury.

Kayshon Boutte|WR.role: Acquired from New England on Aug 24-25, 2026 for S Jaylen Reed and a 2028 seventh-round pick, per Patriots.com. The trade was a direct response to Jayden Higgins tearing his ACL in an Aug 19 joint practice with Las Vegas. His Week 1 role is genuinely unsettled — a pre-trade projected depth chart (Aug 24) had him starting at Z ahead of Xavier Hutchinson, while a Sep 4 Heavy.com piece citing ESPN's Benjamin Solak says he is not expected to be the every-down WR2 to start, with Hutchinson and Jaylin Noel retaining roles while he ramps.
Kayshon Boutte|WR.strength: Led the NFL in first-down-plus-touchdown rate per target at 57.4% in 2025 and ranked 4th in yards per reception among qualifiers. Produced 33/551/6 in 2025 plus a strong postseason (9 catches, 168 yards, 1 TD across four games).
Kayshon Boutte|WR.weakness: A vertical specialist rather than a full-route-tree receiver — 49% of his routes were vertical, 7th-most among WRs — which is not obviously what Houston wants from a WR2. Never a high-volume target earner. Roughly two weeks in the building entering Week 1.

Keenan Allen|WR.role: Signed a one-year deal reported up to $8.32M with Indianapolis in August 2026, reuniting with Shane Steichen, his coordinator in San Diego and Los Angeles from 2014-2020. The Colts had just traded WR1 Michael Pittman Jr. to Pittsburgh — Pittman averaged 130 targets and 89 catches over the prior five seasons — and Allen is expected to step into that role. Fox59 reporting has Allen and Josh Downs rotating between slot and perimeter until Alec Pierce is fully healthy.
Keenan Allen|WR.strength: 1,055 career receptions, 12,051 yards and 70 TD across 13 seasons; six-time Pro Bowler. Route-running and separation are the skills that age best. Seven years of prior history with the play-caller is a real, non-obvious edge on install speed.
Keenan Allen|WR.weakness: Age 34, on a one-year prove-it deal with no multi-year commitment from the team. Extensive injury log — hamstring strains in 2019 and 2020, multiple knee issues including a 2016 ACL reconstruction and a 2013 PCL tear. The target hierarchy is not actually settled: Downs and Pierce both have legitimate claims.

Malachi Fields|WR.role: Third-round rookie, No. 74 overall out of Notre Dame (transferred from Virginia). Listed as the starting WR2 opposite Malik Nabers on the Giants' Sep 1 projected depth chart, ahead of veteran Darius Slayton, with Darnell Mooney in the slot and Isaiah Likely used as a big slot. He was PFF's highest-graded and most-targeted Giants receiver in the preseason, with a 153.5 passer rating when targeted, both contested-catch opportunities converted, and the team's only preseason offensive touchdown on a Jaxson Dart fade. Played almost exclusively on the perimeter — one slot snap all preseason.
Malachi Fields|WR.strength: A large-framed target who wins at the catch point, with excellent leaping ability, body control and downfield ball-tracking, plus more open-field fluidity than the size suggests. Best-graded and most-productive Giants receiver of the 2026 preseason.
Malachi Fields|WR.weakness: A 4.61 forty cooled his draft stock and raises speed-for-size questions. PFN frames him as Nabers insurance rather than a standalone weekly starter. Jaxson Dart is still developing and likely to be inconsistent.

Malik Washington|WR.role: Miami's top returning receiver by default after the room was gutted — Tyreek Hill released, Jaylen Waddle traded to Denver (Mar 18, 2026, confirmed on denverbroncos.com). Opened the preseason with the first-team offense and caught all three targets against Washington, including on Miami's first two offensive snaps. Miami added Jalen Tolbert in free agency and drafted three receivers (Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, Kevin Coleman).
Malik Washington|WR.strength: 2025 line of 46 receptions for 317 yards and 3 TD, plus 110 rushing yards and a rushing TD on 17 carries — genuine all-purpose usage. Serves as Miami's primary return man, which adds a scoring dimension and a PPR floor.
Malik Washington|WR.weakness: His 6.9 yards per catch in 2025 was the worst mark among any receiver with 40+ receptions in the league. That is a shallow, underneath-route profile that needs enormous volume to pay off. Target hierarchy behind him is still crowded with Tolbert, Douglas, Bell and Coleman.

Pat Bryant|WR.role: Year two after a 2025 third-round selection (No. 74, Illinois) in which he went 31/378/1 on 49 targets, third among Denver receivers. Now in a four-way scrum for WR3 behind Courtland Sutton and new arrival Jaylen Waddle, against Troy Franklin and Marvin Mims Jr. Denver's first unofficial depth chart lists him WR4 ahead of Franklin, and both FantasyPros (Sep 3) and an Aug 10 camp report have him as the current favorite for the WR3 job.
Pat Bryant|WR.strength: A 6'2" frame gives him a contested-catch and red-zone edge over the 5'11" Mims. College profile was 15.3 yards per reception with a TD every 7.2 catches. Willing run-blocker, and Sean Payton has invoked Michael Thomas as the skill-set comparison. Safety Talanoa Hufanga reportedly called him the team's most improved offensive player this summer.
Pat Bryant|WR.weakness: The target math is brutal — Denver traded for Waddle specifically to feed Bo Nix. Rookie per-target efficiency was modest (31 catches on 49 targets, 12.2 YPC, one TD) against Franklin's stronger 65/709/6 in 2025. Depth-chart standing is contested even in the bullish reports.

Rashod Bateman|WR.role: Projected starter opposite Zay Flowers, with praise from passing-game coordinator Declan Doyle for expanded route diversity in camp. Week 1 availability is unresolved: GM Eric DeCosta said on Sep 2, 2026 that he does not know when the NFL will finalise its review and that the team is preparing for the possibility of opening the season without him.
Rashod Bateman|WR.strength: Established full-time starter in this offense when available, and says he is healthy and doing "things I've never done before" in the new scheme. Efficient in limited 2025 work — 19 receptions for 224 yards and 2 TD at 11.8 per catch. First-round pedigree.
Rashod Bateman|WR.weakness: Games-played history is inconsistent — 13 games in 2025. Zay Flowers is the clear top target. And the availability question overshadows the football: no amount of camp progress matters if he is not on the field.

Ryan Flournoy|WR.role: Year-three WR3 behind CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, ahead of KaVontae Turpin, Jonathan Mingo and Camden Brown. Did not play in the first preseason game — Brian Schottenheimer largely rested starters — but has had extensive camp reps building chemistry with Dak Prescott.
Ryan Flournoy|WR.strength: 2025 line of 40 receptions for 475 yards and 4 TD across 16 games with 4 starts, and 29 of those catches went for first downs — a chain-mover profile rather than an empty-volume one. August camp reports describe sharper route-running and consistent separation in team drills.
Ryan Flournoy|WR.weakness: Structurally capped as the third read behind two alphas. No game logs above roughly 5-6 targets. The breakout reporting is local and enthusiastic rather than statistically grounded.

Tre' Harris|WR.role: Year two, listed WR3 behind Ladd McConkey and Quentin Johnston on the Chargers' Aug 24 depth chart, though Jim Harbaugh reportedly said in camp "I have [Harris] right there with" the two starters. Competing with rookie Brenen Thompson and 2025 fifth-rounder KeAndre Lambert-Smith. Keenan Allen is no longer on the roster.
Tre' Harris|WR.strength: Averaged 5.5 targets in his final two 2025 games when Johnston was out — the flash of a real role when the door opened. Effective run-blocker as a rookie, which keeps him on the field in a more run-committed scheme even before the targets arrive.
Tre' Harris|WR.weakness: Thin rookie production: 30/324/1 on 43 targets. Usage pattern was blocking-and-gadget rather than target-earning — roughly a 49% snap rate with a 7.4% target share and a 44% route rate. Missed preseason reps to injury at exactly the moment he needed to lock the job down.

Tre Tucker|WR.role: The Raiders' clear No. 2 target behind Brock Bowers, who functions as the de facto WR1 despite playing tight end. FantasyPros (Sep 3) says Tucker "enters 2026 with a legitimate chance to emerge as the Raiders' top wide receiver" and that the new staff has praised his leadership. Logged nearly every snap in 2025.
Tre Tucker|WR.strength: Averaged 9.5 fantasy PPG in 2025 and finished a top-48 fantasy WR. Eleven games with 5+ targets. Full-time snap player, which is the durable part of the profile.
Tre Tucker|WR.weakness: Targeted on just 16.2% of routes run in 2025, 78th in the league, at 1.23 yards per route run — both outside the top 75. The 2025 production was one game: a 40.9-point Week 3 was roughly a quarter of his season total, and he hit double digits only three other times. Undersized at 5'8"/182.

AJ Barner|TE.role: Sits atop an unchanged Seattle tight end depth chart entering 2026 — Barner, Elijah Arroyo, Eric Saubert, Nick Kallerup — per CBS Sports reporting dated Sep 3, 2026. Led the room in every major receiving category in 2025 with 52 catches for 519 yards and 6 TD on 68 targets.
AJ Barner|TE.strength: Clear, unchanged TE1 status with no offseason role change reported. The 2025 line is a real floor — 52 catches and 6 TD is startable production in a shallow position. Still on his 2024 fourth-round rookie deal, entering his age-24/25 season.
AJ Barner|TE.weakness: Elijah Arroyo, the 2025 second-round pick, is the direct competition for pass-catching work and reportedly had a productive 2026 preseason after a quiet rookie year (179 receiving yards). Even without unseating Barner, that is a threat to his target share. The room is four deep.

Dalton Schultz|TE.role: Entrenched TE1 and C.J. Stroud's security blanket, on a roughly 97-target pace across three years in Houston with a career-high 82 catches in 2025. With Jayden Higgins lost for the season to a torn ACL in August, Yahoo's Justin Boone (Aug 20) positions him as Stroud's likely No. 2 target early in 2026.
Dalton Schultz|TE.strength: 82 receptions in 2025 tied for third among tight ends, with 777 yards ranking sixth. Durability is the underrated part — two games missed across three seasons in Houston. Finished 11th among TEs in per-game points over the final 13 weeks of 2025.
Dalton Schultz|TE.weakness: No big-play element — a career 7.0 yards per target. Has not scored more than five TDs in a season since 2021. Turns 30 in 2026. And Houston deepened the room this offseason with Foster Moreau in free agency, second-round rookie Max Klare, and a healthier Cade Stover.

Gunnar Helm|TE.role: Becomes Tennessee's clear No. 1 tight end after Chig Okonkwo left for Washington in free agency (FantasyPros, Sep 2). NFL.com's Bucky Brooks named him to his 2026 All-Breakout Team, citing new OC Brian Daboll's history of featuring tight ends.
Gunnar Helm|TE.strength: Set a franchise rookie-tight-end reception record in 2025 with 44 catches for 357 yards and 2 TD, on an 80% catch rate — efficient, not just present. Listed at 6'5"/241, age 23. NFL.com singles out a Week 15 2025 34-yard touchdown from Cam Ward as the big-play evidence.
Gunnar Helm|TE.weakness: Played in a Tennessee passing offense that struggled for much of 2025 — the efficiency came in a bad environment, which cuts both ways. Daniel Bellinger was brought in from the Giants by Daboll and may take blocking-down snaps (lower confidence, search summary only). His per-target profile is year-one data only.

Kenyon Sadiq|TE.role: The No. 16 overall pick in the 2026 draft, and one of four Jets tight ends alongside 2025 second-rounder Mason Taylor, Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods. OC Frank Reich describes the group as deliberately deep and rotational — "we don't have 11 starters on offense, we got like 15" (Jets.com, Aug 29). FantasyPros (Sep 2) projects him as a low-end TE2 or high-end TE3 and calls him likely undraftable in most redraft leagues.
Kenyon Sadiq|TE.strength: Elite athletic testing — a 4.39 forty — which NFL.com and CBS describe as the fastest by a tight end since at least 2003, the era of reliably comparable electronic timing, rather than the fastest ever outright, with a 43.5-inch vertical. Set an Oregon single-season tight end reception record (51 catches, 560 yards) and led all FBS tight ends with 8 receiving touchdowns in 2025.
Kenyon Sadiq|TE.weakness: Middling college efficiency for a top-16 pick at 1.62 yards per route run. Sits behind Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell, Omar Cooper Jr. and Breece Hall in the target hierarchy. And he has missed nearly all of camp.

Terrance Ferguson|TE.role: Year two (2025 second-rounder, No. 46) in a four-deep, committee Rams tight end room with Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and rookie Max Klare, and no clear-cut TE1. FantasyPros (Sep 3) reports his projected target share was bumped from 9% to 10%, 28th among tight ends, with coaches raving about his ability to line up all over the formation. Yahoo (Sep 4) has him at 18% ownership.
Terrance Ferguson|TE.strength: Led all tight ends in yards per reception in 2025 at 20.8, on a 17.6 average depth of target, and was targeted on 32.4% of his deep routes (12 of 37) — the highest rate among tight ends with 15+ such routes. He played as a slot receiver more than an in-line tight end as a rookie, which is where the fantasy value at this position comes from.
Terrance Ferguson|TE.weakness: Modest rookie counting stats — 11 catches for 231 yards and 3 TD on 25 targets across 14 games. The four-man room dilutes any weekly floor. Higbee signed a two-year extension, so the competition is not going away.

T.J. Hockenson|TE.role: Full-time starter working with the first-team offense, and he connected with new starter Kyler Murray for three touchdowns in a condensed seven-on-seven period at an Aug 17, 2026 practice. But he played just five snaps in the preseason opener and was rested for the final two exhibitions. ADP sits around TE22.
T.J. Hockenson|TE.strength: Availability recovered — 15 games in 2025 after missing seven the year before. Flashed genuine red-zone chemistry with Murray in camp. Former first-round pick with a proven top-five-at-the-position ceiling from his Detroit years.
T.J. Hockenson|TE.weakness: Three touchdowns in 2025, and no catch of 35+ yards in over three years — PFN reads that as athletic decline entering his age-29 season. Career-low 8.6 yards per reception in 2025. PFN ranks him 29th among tight ends, arguing his fantasy appeal does not match his name recognition.

Cairo Santos|K.role: Starter by default — Chicago carries no other kicker on the roster — but the least secure hold of any non-Loop kicker here. CBS Sports explicitly flags that the team could move on given his lack of leg strength.
Cairo Santos|K.strength: Perfect on all 39 PAT attempts in 2025 and hit a game-winning 48-yarder as time expired against Minnesota in Week 11. A 12-year veteran with a clutch track record, kicking for an ascending offense in Ben Johnson's second year.
Cairo Santos|K.weakness: 2025 was uneven — 25 of 30 on field goals (83%) including 4 of 6 from 50-plus, and he missed two games with a thigh injury. Below-average leg strength relative to the position caps his ceiling on longer attempts and is the stated reason Chicago could upgrade.

Cam Little|K.role: Entrenched starter with no camp competition, entering his third season as Jacksonville's kicker with rising stock tied to Liam Coen's improving offense.
Cam Little|K.strength: 2025 line of 30 of 34 on field goals (88%), 50 of 51 on PATs, and 8 makes from 50-plus, including the NFL-record 68-yarder. Finished 5th among all kickers in fantasy scoring and closed the season with double-digit fantasy points in five straight games as the offense improved.
Cam Little|K.weakness: FantasyPros' Week 1 model flags Jacksonville's red-zone efficiency at 25th of 32 — good for field-goal volume, but it signals an offense that swings with game script. Week 1 total sits at a relatively low 40.5.

Cameron Dicker|K.role: Unquestioned starter and reigning first-time Pro Bowler, no camp competition. FantasyPros' Week 1 rankings (Sep 2, 2026) have him as the No. 1 fantasy kicker.
Cameron Dicker|K.strength: 92.7% on field goals in 2025 including 5 of 6 from 50-plus, and 97.1% on PATs; he is the most accurate kicker in NFL history — he took the record on Sep 15, 2025 at 94 of 100 career field goals (94.0%), passing Justin Tucker's 89.1%, and has since tracked in the 93.8-94.1% range. Has hit a 59-yarder in each of the last two seasons and is 21 of 27 career from 50-plus.
Cameron Dicker|K.weakness: A more explosive offense under new OC Mike McDaniel could mean more touchdowns and fewer short field goals. Elite accuracy leaves little margin — the value is volume-dependent on Chargers drives stalling.

Eddy Pineiro|K.role: Entrenched starter coming off a four-year, $17M extension signed in March 2026, with no reported camp competition.
Eddy Pineiro|K.strength: Led all qualified kickers with a 96.6% field-goal rate in 2025, pushing his career mark to 89.7%, second all-time. Averaged 10.0 fantasy points per game, tied 5th among kickers with 6-plus games.
Eddy Pineiro|K.weakness: San Francisco's red-zone efficiency ranked 29th of 32 in FantasyPros' Week 1 model — framed as a positive for field-goal volume, but it also reflects an offense whose output has been inconsistent because of skill-position injuries.

Jake Bates|K.role: Entrenched starter with no camp competition, entering his third season as a clear top-10 fantasy kicker target despite a new offensive coordinator.
Jake Bates|K.strength: Led the NFL in extra points in each of his first two seasons — 64 in 2024 and 54 in 2025 — which is a direct readout of how much this offense scores. Real range: 4 of 9 from 50-plus in 2025 with the misses coming from 67 and 65. Career marks of 84.1% on field goals and 95.9% on PATs.
Jake Bates|K.weakness: Dan Campbell's fourth-down aggression actively removes field-goal attempts inside Detroit's scoring range. A high-efficiency offense that scores touchdowns rather than settling for three caps the field-goal ceiling even as it raises the PAT floor.

Jason Myers|K.role: Entrenched starter and the 2025 fantasy K1, no camp competition. FantasyPros' Sep 2, 2026 Week 1 piece calls him the "2025 kicker MVP."
Jason Myers|K.strength: Led all fantasy kickers in 2025 with 202.0 points, setting a career high in field goals while going a perfect 48 for 48 on PATs and converting 41 of 48 field goals. Has led the NFL in attempts in two of the last three seasons.
Jason Myers|K.weakness: The year-to-year swings are the story: 24th in 2021, 1st in 2022, 5th in 2023, 18th in 2024, 1st in 2025. FantasyPros' own kicker analyst flags this as reason to expect regression despite ranking him top-five.

Ka'imi Fairbairn|K.role: Entrenched, low-risk starter with no camp competition, entering his ninth season. FantasyPros rates him a top-two fantasy kicker for 2026.
Ka'imi Fairbairn|K.strength: Led all kickers with 12.9 fantasy points per game in 2025, and led the NFL in both attempts (48) and makes (44) despite missing two games. 91.3% accuracy and 97.3% on PATs over the last four years, with a strong 73.9% (51 of 69) career mark from 50-plus. Houston led the NFL with 52 team field-goal attempts in 2025.
Ka'imi Fairbairn|K.weakness: Houston scored touchdowns on just 45.9% of red-zone trips in 2025 — good for his volume, but newly acquired David Montgomery (29 red-zone rushing TDs since 2023) is specifically the kind of addition that converts those trips into touchdowns instead of field goals. Tough fantasy-playoff slate at Philadelphia and at Green Bay.

Tyler Loop|K.role: Starter as of the most current reporting, but the job is genuinely shaky — this is the least secure situation of any kicker in this band. HC Jesse Minter said on Sep 1, 2026, "I expect him to be our kicker going into Indy," but Baltimore signed veteran Jake Moody to the practice squad on Sep 2 after Loop missed kicks late in the preseason. He was not released in the initial 53-man cuts. On the predecessor: Justin Tucker, Baltimore's kicker from 2012-2024, was released by the Ravens on May 5, 2025 in a move the team framed as a football decision (baltimoreravens.com). The NFL's 10-game Personal Conduct Policy suspension was announced separately and afterward, while he was already a free agent — the release did not follow the suspension. He has denied the allegations and remained unsigned as of Jan 2026. Loop was the 6th-round pick drafted to replace him and won the job outright in August 2025.
Tyler Loop|K.strength: Genuine leg strength — an Arizona program-record 62-yarder in college, and makes from 51, 53 and 61 in his 2025 preseason.
Tyler Loop|K.weakness: Missed 3 of 8 preseason field goals in 2025 camp, all beyond 50 and all at his home stadium, and struggled on kickoffs late in his rookie year. Missed a 44-yard game-winner against Pittsburgh late in 2025 that ended Baltimore's playoff hopes — a clutch narrative raised on the record by beat reporter Jason La Canfora and an anonymous NFL personnel executive.

Baltimore Ravens|DST.role: Coming off a poor 2025 — 24th overall and 30th against the pass under then-DC Zach Orr — but projected top-10 to 12 for 2026 by some outlets. A talent-driven bounce-back bet, not a proven set-and-forget.
Baltimore Ravens|DST.strength: Retains Kyle Hamilton, Roquan Smith, Marlon Humphrey, Nate Wiggins, Malaki Starks and Nnamdi Madubuike. Signed DE Trey Hendrickson away from Cincinnati at four years, $112M; the Hendrickson-Smith-Hamilton trio ranked top-10 in one defensive-triplets preview.
Baltimore Ravens|DST.weakness: The 2025 performance was genuinely bad, and the bounce-back thesis rests on new leadership rather than on results. A simultaneous head-coach and coordinator change is one of the largest hidden risks a fantasy defense can carry.

Denver Broncos|DST.role: A top-5 fantasy D/ST and one of the few genuine weekly starters at the position rather than a streamer, after finishing around the No. 4-6 defense per game in 2025.
Denver Broncos|DST.strength: Nik Bonitto put up 14 sacks on a 19.4% pressure rate, second among qualified rushers in 2025. Pat Surtain II — the 2024 Defensive Player of the Year — anchors the secondary. The unit led the NFL with 68 sacks and allowed the third-fewest points at 18.3 per game.
Denver Broncos|DST.weakness: The scoring profile is heavily pass-rush dependent, so a sack regression from a league-leading 68 hits the fantasy line directly. Surtain missed almost all of November 2025. Run-defense detail did not surface in this pass.

Green Bay Packers|DST.role: Ranked anywhere from 12th to 24th depending on source — a streamer to open the season because the best defender is out, with real upside once he returns.
Green Bay Packers|DST.strength: Micah Parsons headlines the unit once healthy. Added DT Javon Hargrave and CB Benjamin St-Juste in free agency, traded for LB Zaire Franklin, and spent the first three 2026 draft picks on defense.
Green Bay Packers|DST.weakness: Parsons opened the season on Reserve/PUP recovering from a torn ACL suffered in Week 15 of 2025 (surgery Dec 29) and is out at least the first four games — his own optimistic target is Week 6 against Dallas, with Week 8 seen as more realistic. Also lost EDGE Rashan Gary, thinning the rush further in Parsons' absence.

Jacksonville Jaguars|DST.role: Ranked roughly 17th to 21st in 2026 D/ST projections — a matchup streamer built on takeaways rather than pressure, not a draftable set-and-forget.
Jacksonville Jaguars|DST.strength: Second in the NFL with 22 interceptions in 2025 and led the league in passes defended. Travis Hunter could add real ceiling if used full-time at corner in 2026.
Jacksonville Jaguars|DST.weakness: Shaky third-down defense, poor pressure rate and few sacks in 2025 — the takeaway total was not supported by an underlying pass rush, which is the classic non-repeatable profile. Lost LB Devin Lloyd, S Andrew Wingard and CB Greg Newsome this offseason.

Kansas City Chiefs|DST.role: Described as hardly fantasy-relevant in 2025 and now further weakened at cornerback — a streamer at best, leaning on schedule rather than talent.
Kansas City Chiefs|DST.strength: Steve Spagnuolo remains DC, providing scheme continuity in a year of turnover elsewhere. Some defensive-line additions this offseason. A favorable early schedule — one outlet rated it the third-easiest opening slate.
Kansas City Chiefs|DST.weakness: Lost two-time All-Pro CB Trent McDuffie and CB Jaylen Watson, both traded to the Rams. Losing both starting outside corners in a single offseason on a unit that was already not elite is a severe, hard-to-replace drain.

Los Angeles Chargers|DST.role: A low-end No. 1 fantasy D/ST worth a late-round pick, after finishing 11th in D/ST scoring in 2025.
Los Angeles Chargers|DST.strength: Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu anchor a rush that produced 45 sacks in 2025. Derwin James headlines the secondary. The unit posted 19 interceptions (tied 3rd) and allowed 18.9 points per game (7th-fewest).
Los Angeles Chargers|DST.weakness: A brand-new coordinator with no prior NFL primary play-calling experience. First-round 2026 capital went to another edge rusher in Akheem Mesidor, which suggests the front office also sees a gap.

Los Angeles Rams|DST.role: Ranked a top-3 fantasy D/ST for 2026 after an extraordinary offseason talent influx, trending toward an early-round pick rather than a streamer — with the caveat that the group has zero game reps together.
Los Angeles Rams|DST.strength: Traded for Myles Garrett, the 2025 Defensive Player of the Year, sending Jared Verse plus picks to Cleveland. Aaron Donald came out of retirement on a one-year, $20M deal. Traded for CB Trent McDuffie, a two-time All-Pro, and extended him at four years, $124M. The 2025 unit was already 4th in pressure rate, 10th in sack rate and around the 5th-best fantasy defense before any of that.
Los Angeles Rams|DST.weakness: Garrett, Donald and McDuffie have never played a snap together — chemistry and fit are genuine unknowns. Donald is returning after two years away with uncertain snap counts. Heavy trade capital spent may have thinned depth.

Minnesota Vikings|DST.role: Ranked roughly 7th to 11th across 2026 D/ST projections — a solid flex or high-end streamer built on Brian Flores' pressure scheme rather than on personnel dominance.
Minnesota Vikings|DST.strength: Led the NFL in pressure rate at 44.5% in 2025. Allowed touchdowns on just 15.5% of drives, third-best in the league. The blitz-heavy design creates high-variance takeaway upside, which is what pays in D/ST scoring.
Minnesota Vikings|DST.weakness: Lost EDGE Jonathan Greenard, traded to Philadelphia — a real subtraction from the pass rush with no clearly named direct replacement. The scheme can be boom-bust against quick-passing offenses that neutralise the blitz.

New England Patriots|DST.role: 2025 AFC champions who lost Super Bowl LX to Seattle, and posted a top-10 fantasy finish behind a historically soft schedule. Multiple outlets now flag them as a regression candidate given a brutal 2026 slate — a mid-tier streamer, not set-and-forget.
New England Patriots|DST.strength: CB Christian Gonzalez broke out with a league-low 43.4% completion rate allowed when targeted in 2025 and anchors a secondary PFF ranks No. 1 league-wide for 2026. Christian Barmore and Milton Williams are both finally healthy for a full season on the interior line.
New England Patriots|DST.weakness: No proven high-end edge rusher, per multiple outlets. Coordinator turnover — original hire Terrell Williams stepped away mid-2025 while being treated for prostate cancer, with ILB coach Zak Kuhr elevated. 2026 is Kuhr's first full season calling plays.

Seattle Seahawks|DST.role: Reigning Super Bowl LX champions and 2025's No. 1-scoring fantasy D/ST, returning 10 of 11 starters — a genuine set-and-forget option.
Seattle Seahawks|DST.strength: Leonard Williams was ESPN's top-ranked defensive tackle with 7 sacks, an 11.5% pressure rate and 12 run stuffs in 2025. Devon Witherspoon ranked 4th among corners. The unit led the NFL in points allowed per game at 17.2 and tied for 4th in the NFC with 47 sacks.
Seattle Seahawks|DST.weakness: Repeating as the No. 1-scoring fantasy defense is historically rare — regression is the base case, not a bear case. No single double-digit sack rusher (three players tied at 7), so the pressure is scheme-driven rather than star-driven, which is less sticky.

Emanuel Wilson|RB.role: Confirmed to have left Green Bay — Seattle signed him on Mar 13, 2026 for one year up to $2.1M after three Packers seasons. He is the third leg of the Price/Holani/Wilson committee assembled after Kenneth Walker III left for Kansas City and Zach Charbonnet went on PUP. RotoBaller projects 12-15 touches per game in September while Charbonnet is out.
Emanuel Wilson|RB.strength: The efficiency profile is genuinely good — an 82.9 PFF overall grade in 2024 and a 73.9 rushing grade in 2025, a 4.5 career yards per carry, a 76.8% yards-after-contact rate in 2025, and per RotoBaller the third-best rushing success rate in the league last season.
Emanuel Wilson|RB.weakness: PFF's own evaluation says he does not offer much in the passing game. Behind a first-round rookie in draft-capital pecking order. Never a full-time starter in Green Bay, so the lead-back sample is thin.

George Holani|RB.role: Listed as the starter on Seattle's first unofficial depth chart (Aug 12, 2026), but the same report cautions he may see most of his snaps on passing downs while rookie first-rounder Jadarian Price takes early-down carries — a three-man committee with Emanuel Wilson while Zach Charbonnet recovers.
George Holani|RB.strength: The staff has repeatedly praised his receiving and pass protection. His role expanded in the 2025 playoffs once Charbonnet went down, with 4 catches for 34 yards over the final two postseason games.
George Holani|RB.weakness: Minimal career workload — 22 carries for 73 yards and a TD across 11 games in 2025. Buried behind a first-round rookie in draft capital and a PFF favourite in Wilson. Low touchdown equity if Price and Wilson take goal-line work.

James Conner|RB.role: Opens 2026 on injured reserve with a designation to return, per Cardinals beat reporter John Gambadoro (Aug 30, 2026) — out a minimum of four games with a foot injury. He had already lost the starting job before the injury: Arizona spent the No. 4 overall pick on Jeremiyah Love and signed Tyler Allgeier.
James Conner|RB.strength: As recently as last season he was a top-16 RB at 15.6 PPR points per game while handling 54.2% of Arizona's rushing attempts. Reworked his contract to stay, and the staff values him as a veteran presence.
James Conner|RB.weakness: Has not practised in team drills through camp — individual work only. No longer atop the depth chart even when healthy. Will have missed a full month by the time he is eligible.

Jaylen Wright|RB.role: Miami's unofficial RB2 behind De'Von Achane on the first camp depth chart released Aug 11, 2026, ahead of 2025 sixth-rounder Ollie Gordon II. CBS's June outlook frames him purely as Achane's backup — the same role as his first two seasons.
Jaylen Wright|RB.strength: Camp reports credit solid pass-catching and good vision between the tackles. OL Aaron Brewer publicly praised his maturity on Aug 11.
Jaylen Wright|RB.weakness: Just 8 career receptions across two NFL seasons, which caps the standalone PPR case even in a starter role. Gordon has flashed more raw power and burst in camp and is a live threat to the RB2 job. CBS is blunt: not worth considering until Achane misses time.

Justice Hill|RB.role: In line to be the No. 2 back behind Derrick Henry to open 2026 (CBS/RotoWire, Aug 24, 2026). He is in the final year of his contract under a new coaching staff, and did not appear in either preseason game — which CBS reads as a sign he is locked into his standing rather than needing reps to prove it.
Justice Hill|RB.strength: Established passing-down role with system familiarity, in an offense that has used him in that capacity for years. Active through offseason work after an injury-shortened 2025.
Justice Hill|RB.weakness: 2025 was cut to 10 games including an IR stint from Nov 27; he had 39 touches before it. Even at full health the ceiling is capped, because Baltimore throws to backs so little that a full-time passing-down role does not translate into fantasy volume.

Kaelon Black|RB.role: 2026 rookie out of Indiana who has climbed into the clear RB2 spot behind Christian McCaffrey after Jordan James fractured a rib in practice, with Isaac Guerendo falling further down the chart (FantasyPros, Sep 4). Made the initial 53 off a strong close to camp.
Kaelon Black|RB.strength: Averaged 5.6 YPC with 10 rushing TDs on under 200 attempts in his final college season. Greg Cosell described him as a physical, no-holds-barred downhill runner. Ran 12 times for 61 yards (5.1 YPC) in the preseason finale.
Kaelon Black|RB.weakness: Did not finish top-40 among FBS backs in yards after contact per attempt, breakaway rate, or PFF elusive rating as a prospect. Not viewed as a receiving-down option. Missed roughly two weeks of camp with an adductor injury.

Kaytron Allen|RB.role: 2026 sixth-round pick (No. 187, Penn State) who made Washington's initial 53 (Sep 1, 2026), beating out UDFA Robert Henry Jr. Sits third behind Rachaad White and Jacory Croskey-Merritt, positioned for short-yardage and red-zone work.
Kaytron Allen|RB.strength: In his preseason debut he ran 23 times for 85 yards and a touchdown, and per Warren Sharp became the only back in the last decade to record 20+ preseason carries without a single negative-yardage run. At 5'11"/216 he is the biggest back on the roster, filling the power void left by Chris Rodriguez Jr.'s departure to Jacksonville.
Kaytron Allen|RB.weakness: Bleacher Report's Gary Davenport flagged that he lacks game-breaking explosiveness and needs pass-protection refinement. The preseason debut came at a modest 3.7 YPC despite the zero-negative-run streak.

Malik Davis|RB.role: The clear-cut RB2 behind Javonte Williams after Dallas waived both Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah at final cutdown, following a preseason in which Davis outperformed Blue on efficiency (SI, Aug 24, 2026). FantasyPros has him at RB #205 ECR with an ADP around #262 — handcuff-only pricing.
Malik Davis|RB.strength: Efficient in his 2025 work — 250 yards on 52 carries (4.8 YPC) at a 50% success rate across 10 games with zero fumbles. Added 29 yards on 5 carries plus an 8-yard receiving TD this preseason. A Fort Worth Star-Telegram beat writer specifically credited his pass protection as the thing separating him from Blue.
Malik Davis|RB.weakness: Age 27, a career journeyman with essentially no explosive-play profile. FantasyPros projects 62.4 carries and 45.6 total fantasy points for the whole season.

Najee Harris|RB.role: Signed a one-year deal with the Giants on Aug 18, 2026. The path there: four Pittsburgh seasons with 1,000-plus rushing yards each year, a one-year Chargers deal in 2025, a torn Achilles in Week 3 of 2025 that ended his season, then free agency. The Giants kept four backs on the initial 53 — Cam Skattebo as starter, plus Harris, Tyrone Tracy Jr. and Devin Singletary as effective co-No. 2s.
Najee Harris|RB.strength: A proven 1,000-yard workhorse in each of his four Pittsburgh seasons. Made his Giants preseason debut Aug 28 with 11 carries for 39 yards plus a 20-yard catch on his lone target, and was the first back to touch the ball in that game.
Najee Harris|RB.weakness: By his own admission on Aug 19 he is "not fully in football shape," distinguishing conditioning from football shape. Buried behind an incumbent starter in Skattebo with no defined pass-game role.

Antonio Williams|WR.role: Reached Washington via the draft, not a trade — a third-round pick (No. 71, 2026) out of Clemson. He was tabbed to win the No. 3 job behind Terry McLaurin and newly signed Stefon Diggs, competing with Van Jefferson, Dyami Brown, Treylon Burks and Luke McCaffrey for snaps.
Antonio Williams|WR.strength: Led Clemson in receptions in each of his last two seasons, totalling 208 catches for 2,336 yards and 21 TD over four years. Diggs himself praised him after an August practice: "he can hoop a little bit; he got some game." Strong short-area quickness and separation, useful on screens and gadget plays.
Antonio Williams|WR.weakness: Ranked 69th nationally in yards per route run and 39th in receiving grade in his final college season as an underneath slot option. Not a vertical threat, with drop issues in college. And the Diggs signing directly downgraded him — FantasyPros' Derek Brown: "Antonio Williams' rookie season outlook took a massive hit... I wouldn't count on him as anything more than a bye-week flex option unless Diggs gets hurt."

Caleb Douglas|WR.role: Third-round rookie (No. 75, Texas Tech) listed among Miami's top three receivers alongside Malik Washington and Jalen Tolbert on the Dolphins' first camp depth chart under HC Jeff Hafley. With Tyreek Hill released and Jaylen Waddle traded to Denver, the WR1/2 competition is genuinely open and Douglas has reportedly won a first-team spot early. TE Greg Dulcich called him "a stud."
Caleb Douglas|WR.strength: Elite testing — a 4.39 forty and a 9.50 Relative Athletic Score. Led Texas Tech in receiving as a Second Team All-Big 12 pick with 846 yards in his final college season. Forced 17 missed tackles over his last two seasons with good hip sink for a 6'4" frame.
Caleb Douglas|WR.weakness: The efficiency metrics are poor — 158th and 116th nationally in yards per route run over his last two college seasons, a 44th-percentile dominator rating and a 37th-percentile breakout age, with only 5.4 and 5.9 yards after catch per reception. FantasyPros' Derek Brown is explicitly skeptical: "They must see something that I don't... I'll leave him on the board for others to draft."

Darnell Mooney|WR.role: Signed a one-year deal worth up to $10M with the Giants in March 2026 after Atlanta released him as a cap casualty, saving them $18.4M. He joined a crowded room with Malik Nabers and Darius Slayton. As of Aug 21, 2026 the Giants have fielded trade calls from multiple teams about him, and he was conspicuously absent from the field in the preseason win over Miami.
Darnell Mooney|WR.strength: A proven WR2 ceiling — 64 catches for 992 yards and 5 TD with Atlanta in 2024, and 1,435 yards over two Atlanta seasons.
Darnell Mooney|WR.weakness: 2025 was a washout — a training-camp shoulder injury limited him to 32 catches for 443 yards and 1 TD on 72 targets across 15 games, never topping four catches in a game.

Devaughn Vele|WR.role: Entering his third season, normally the Saints' WR3 behind Chris Olave and rookie Jordyn Tyson — but with Tyson sidelined by a hamstring, FantasyPros (Sep 3, 2026) projects him into an expanded role and effectively New Orleans' No. 2 receiver for the Sep 13 opener against Detroit.
Devaughn Vele|WR.strength: Finished 2025 strong — 19 of 26 targets for 239 yards and a TD over his final four games, averaging just under 10 half-PPR points per game across that stretch, with minimum WR4 production in all four. Direct beneficiary of Tyson's injury for a real Week 1 bump. Established rapport with Tyler Shough from the second half of 2025.
Devaughn Vele|WR.weakness: Buried in a room the Saints deliberately restocked — Tyson, Bryce Lance and Barion Brown all arrived this offseason. Modest full-season 2025 output of 293 yards and 2 TD outside the hot close. Shoulder injury history including a prior IR stint.

Germie Bernard|WR.role: Pittsburgh traded up with Indianapolis to take the Alabama receiver at No. 47 overall in 2026. He entered camp behind DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr., then earned first-team reps in August with incumbent Roman Wilson dropping to the second team, and caught 4 of 5 targets for 51 yards in his preseason debut. Athlon and Steelers Depot both frame him as having won the WR3 job.
Germie Bernard|WR.strength: Strong college finish — 64 catches for 862 yards and 7 TD as an Alabama senior in 2025. Lined up everywhere in camp: slot, outside, even the backfield. Beat his direct competitor head-to-head in preseason reps.
Germie Bernard|WR.weakness: Rookie learning curve behind two established veterans. A WR3 ceiling in a run-first offense with a 42-year-old quarterback caps the weekly target share.

Keon Coleman|WR.role: Entering year three as a former No. 33 overall pick (2024) who has not become a clear No. 1 or even a stable weekly target earner — which is the answer to why a former second-rounder sits this low. Buffalo traded a second-round pick to Chicago for D.J. Moore (plus a 2026 fifth) and drafted WR Skyler Bell in the fourth round, both moves that squeeze his share.
Keon Coleman|WR.strength: Flashed a real ceiling as a rookie — a 19.2 yards-per-catch average and 4 TD on just 29 catches in 2024. Had a genuine standout as recently as Week 1 of 2025: 8 catches, 112 yards, a TD against Baltimore. Joe Brady publicly says he still has high hopes and expects a big leap.
Keon Coleman|WR.weakness: After that Week 1 game he failed to top 49 receiving yards in any game the rest of the season and was benched or inactive multiple times. Full 2025 line: 38 catches on 59 targets for 404 yards and 4 TD in 13 games. CBS is blunt — he "scored 25.2 PPR points in Week 1 last year, then averaged 6.4 PPR points per game from Weeks 2 through 18... Fantasy managers should be able to move past him."

Tank Dell|WR.role: Confirmed — Houston placed Dell on injured reserve at the Aug 30, 2026 cutdown. He is ineligible to return before Week 5, so he is out Weeks 1-4 minimum. GM Nick Caserio said around that time that Dell is "close, but not quite there." He simultaneously agreed to a reworked one-year, $1.7M deal with $1M guaranteed, down from a roughly $3.6M final rookie-deal year.
Tank Dell|WR.strength: Explosive slot role and real big-play chemistry with C.J. Stroud in his 2023 rookie season. Retains full playbook familiarity if activated.
Tank Dell|WR.weakness: Has not played a game since Week 16 of 2024 — multiple torn knee ligaments and a dislocated kneecap — and missed all of 2025. Requires a designation to return plus a practice window before any Week 5 activation.

Ted Hurst III|WR.role: Third-round pick (No. 84, 2026) out of Georgia State after transferring from Valdosta State. Emeka Egbuka and Chris Godwin are the starters; the WR3 job was open behind them, and GM Jason Licht confirmed after the 53 was set that Hurst "is going to play a role this year," having exceeded the expectations Licht held on draft day. He competes with Jalen McMillan and Tez Johnson for it.
Ted Hurst III|WR.strength: Licht's own quote traces the rise: "I personally thought... may not make a big impact for us this year but, one for the future... he's proven to us throughout camp... he's going to play a role" (Sep 1, 2026). At 6'4"/206 he partially offsets Mike Evans' departure to San Francisco as a contested-catch X option.
Ted Hurst III|WR.weakness: Unproven with no regular-season snaps. Behind two established starters and competing directly with McMillan, who has starting-caliber pedigree when healthy. Tampa Bay's receiver room has been injury-prone — Evans, Godwin and McMillan all missed significant 2025 time — which cuts both ways.

Troy Franklin|WR.role: Entering year three out of Oregon. CBS's June outlook expected him to win the No. 3 job behind Courtland Sutton and newly traded-for Jaylen Waddle, but Denver's first unofficial depth chart (Aug 12, 2026) actually lists Marvin Mims Jr. ahead of him, with Franklin sharing second-team snaps with Lil'Jordan Humphrey — a demotion from the No. 2 role he held in 2025.
Troy Franklin|WR.strength: The 2025 floor was real — 65 catches for 709 yards and 6 TD on 104-106 targets as Denver's clear No. 2 behind Sutton. Still only 23, with college chemistry from his Oregon years with Bo Nix.
Troy Franklin|WR.weakness: He faded badly down the stretch: 81 targets and a 22% share entering the Week 12 bye, then only 24 targets and a 9% share over his final seven games including playoffs. Then he got passed on the depth chart in August.

Zachariah Branch|WR.role: Falcons third-round pick (No. 79, 2026) out of Georgia after transferring from USC. Post-draft depth charts put him fourth behind Drake London, Jahan Dotson and Olamide Zaccheaus, but his clearest runway is the slot/F spot Zaccheaus holds — Atlanta plans to move him across all three alignments. FantasyPros has him fourth in the target pecking order behind London, Kyle Pitts and Bijan Robinson.
Zachariah Branch|WR.strength: Elite open-field and YAC ability plus real return-game value with multiple return TDs in college. Produced 81 catches for 811 yards and 6 TD at Georgia in 2025 after 78 catches over two USC seasons. Genuine alignment versatility — backfield, slot, bunch and stack.
Zachariah Branch|WR.weakness: Undersized at 5'10"/180 with a limited catch radius; struggles in contested and tight man coverage. Minimal blocking value. Fourth in a target hierarchy behind three established weapons.

Cade Otton|TE.role: Entrenched as Tampa Bay's every-down TE1 — he led all NFL tight ends in snap share in 2025 — and the Buccaneers added no draft or free-agent competition at the position. Mike Evans' departure to San Francisco theoretically opens targets, but Chris Godwin, Jalen McMillan, sophomore Emeka Egbuka and third-round rookie Ted Hurst III all compete for the same share.
Cade Otton|TE.strength: A consistent target earner with 59 receptions in each of the last two seasons. Has shown a genuine spike-week ceiling when the receiver room thins — 30 catches for 293 yards and 3 TD over a four-game stretch in 2024 with Evans and Godwin both out.
Cade Otton|TE.weakness: Just one receiving touchdown in 2025 on 572 yards, a TE25 finish. Has finished 25th or worse in fantasy points per game in three of his four pro seasons. No athletic or red-zone profile that separates him from the streaming pack.

Evan Engram|TE.role: Remains Denver's primary tight end with Adam Trautman as the blocking complement, but CBS states plainly he "should remain the primary tight end for the Broncos this season, but he's not worth drafting in the majority of leagues."
Evan Engram|TE.strength: The résumé has a genuine elite ceiling — he finished second in PPR tight end scoring in 2023 at 232.3 points. Sean Payton has moved him around the formation rather than treating him as a pure slot receiver.
Evan Engram|TE.weakness: 2025 was a broad failure in year one with Denver — 50 catches for 461 yards and 1 TD on 76 targets, with exactly one end-zone target in 16 games and not a single 50-yard game. PFN frames his fantasy relevance as having "gone the way of the dinosaur."

Greg Dulcich|TE.role: The presumptive TE1 and the lone holdover from Miami's 2025 tight end group after Darren Waller and Julian Hill both left. GM Jon-Eric Sullivan named him the player he is most looking forward to seeing make a big move in 2026 (SI, Jul 15, 2026).
Greg Dulcich|TE.strength: Strong per-catch efficiency in his Miami sample — 26 catches for 335 yards (12.9 average) and a TD in 10 games with 3 starts in 2025, with essentially all of it coming in the second half once he took the starting role. That pace projects to roughly 50 catches over a full season.
Greg Dulcich|TE.weakness: Only 31 career games and 13 starts across four seasons and three organisations. Had to sign to Miami's practice squad in August 2025 after being released by the Giants before working onto the active roster — a journeyman profile with no full season of lead-tight-end volume.

Pat Freiermuth|TE.role: Clear TE1 now that Jonnu Smith and his 38 targets are off the roster, with Darnell Washington the blocking-oriented TE2. Steelers Depot (Jun 30, 2026) finds it "hard to imagine Freiermuth not playing at least 60% of the Steelers' offensive snaps in 2026," up from a career-low 51.6% in 2025.
Pat Freiermuth|TE.strength: Zero drops on 54 targets in 2025, with a career-long 68-yard catch. Owns three 60-plus catch seasons and three years averaging 10-plus yards per reception. Above-average pass blocker.
Pat Freiermuth|TE.weakness: Snap share collapsed to 51.6% in 2025 while splitting with Jonnu Smith. Run blocking grades only average and is not expected to improve. And the structural problem: Rodgers has never had a tight end top 767 receiving yards in a season he quarterbacked.

Andy Borregales|K.role: Entrenched starter who won the job as a 2025 sixth-round rookie over veteran John Parker Romo. Patriots.com lists him solo at kicker with no camp competition.
Andy Borregales|K.strength: A historic rookie season — 134 points in 2025, tied for seventh-most in the NFL and the most ever by a Patriots rookie. Real leg strength: 4 of 4 from 50-plus including a 53-yard game-sealer and a 52-yard game-winner at Buffalo, with a career-long 59 against Miami.
Andy Borregales|K.weakness: Only 84.4% on field goals overall (27 of 32), below the elite tier, and a shaky 7 of 11 (63.6%) from 40-49 — the wrong zone to be weak in. The playoffs were rockier still at 4 of 6 across four games.

Chase McLaughlin|K.role: Entrenched multi-year starter and the franchise's most accurate kicker ever at 90.1% career field-goal rate, with no competition mentioned anywhere in Pewter Report's dedicated 2026 preview (Jul 27, 2026). Entering the final year of his contract, which the piece frames as a storyline rather than a job-security threat.
Chase McLaughlin|K.strength: Franchise-record 90.1% accuracy as a Buccaneer, and a franchise-record 65-yard field goal in Week 4 of 2025. Elite long range — 11 of 12 (91.7%) from 50-plus in 2025, after 7 of 8 and 8 of 10 in his first two Tampa seasons.
Chase McLaughlin|K.weakness: 2025 was his least accurate Buccaneers season at 32 of 38 (84.2%), the first year under 90% since 2022, with four of his six misses clustered in Weeks 1-6.

Evan McPherson|K.role: Unquestioned starter with no camp competition reported. FantasyPros (Sep 4, 2026) notes he is tied to one of the best offenses in the NFL if Joe Burrow stays healthy.
Evan McPherson|K.strength: Bounced back sharply in 2025 to a career-high 89.3% accuracy, up from a career-low 72.7% in 2024. Improved markedly from distance — 15 of 18 from 40-plus in 2025 against 6 of 12 in 2024.
Evan McPherson|K.weakness: FantasyPros flags that he still ranked only 12th in field-goal percentage despite the bounce-back — mid-pack, not elite. Volume is entirely offense-dependent.

Harrison Mevis|K.role: Holds the job outright, and notably the Rams added no kicker competition for 2026 despite three years of instability at the position (SI, Jun 8, 2026). On the predecessor: Joshua Karty, the 2024 draftee who held the job roughly a season and a half, lost it mid-2025 after two blocked kicks against Philadelphia — one a potential game-winner — and a missed 53-yarder in a loss to San Francisco. The Rams waived Karty outright once Mevis stabilised the role. A clean succession, not an open competition.
Harrison Mevis|K.strength: Went 12 of 13 (92.3%) in the 2025 regular season after taking over, and hit the game-winning overtime field goal in the playoffs against Chicago. Perfect 2 for 2 beyond 50.
Harrison Mevis|K.weakness: A very small sample — 9 appearances and 13 attempts. His one miss came from just 48 yards, and SI flags that the Rams rarely tested him beyond 50, so the long-range proof is thin. The same beat piece notes it is "very possible the Rams are looking for a kicker at some point during the season" if he struggles.

Buffalo Bills|DST.role: FantasyPros' Sep 4, 2026 table has Buffalo at DST15 with a range of 11-20 — a streamer and matchup unit rather than a locked-in draft target, with real uncertainty priced in given the offseason overhaul.
Buffalo Bills|DST.strength: Bradley Chubb signed a three-year, $43.5M deal to rush opposite Greg Rousseau, who logged 7 sacks and a 15.4% pressure rate (14th) in 2025. Christian Benford and Cole Bishop return as clear-cut secondary anchors, reinforced by free-agent signings Dee Alford, Geno Stone and C.J. Gardner-Johnson.
Buffalo Bills|DST.weakness: CB Taron Johnson was traded away, and CB2 is an open competition between Maxwell Hairston and Davison Igbinosun — an unsettled starting spot entering Week 1. That much roster turnover on top of a scheme change is a lot of variance.

Cleveland Browns|DST.role: FantasyPros' Sep 4, 2026 table ranks Cleveland DST16 with a wide 12-25 range — a late-round flier and streamer, not a draft priority. Other outlets converge around the same tier.
Cleveland Browns|DST.strength: Denzel Ward remains a Pro Bowl-caliber corner anchoring a secondary that also has S Grant Delpit. The Greg Newsome trade return, CB Tyson Campbell, was solid across 12 Cleveland games, allowing 6.4 yards per target in coverage.
Cleveland Browns|DST.weakness: The major one: Cleveland traded Myles Garrett — fresh off setting the NFL single-season sack record with 23 in 2025 — to the Rams for Jared Verse plus draft compensation. Verse is a strong bull rusher but this is not a like-for-like swap. ESPN put it bluntly: it will take a collective effort to replace 23 sacks, and Cleveland is expected to fall off its 13th-ranked 2025 points-allowed finish.

Detroit Lions|DST.role: FantasyPros' Sep 4, 2026 consensus rankings slot Detroit at DST13 with a range of 8-20 and a standard deviation of 5 — notable analyst disagreement, so a matchup-flexible unit rather than draft-and-forget. A separate FantasyPros staff note calls them a sleeper to take with your last pick, citing the easiest schedule in the NFL, specifically through the first five weeks.
Detroit Lions|DST.strength: Aidan Hutchinson is coming off a career-high 14.5 sacks and Detroit ranked 4th in the NFL with 49 total sacks in 2025. FantasyPros credits the unit with the 4th-most passes defended and a top-10 DVOA defense, plus the 2nd-most dropped interceptions (9) — a genuine takeaway-luck rebound case.
Detroit Lions|DST.weakness: Only 13 interceptions actually converted in 2025 despite the passes-defended volume, so the takeaway upside is a "should be better" profile rather than a demonstrated one. And the secondary health situation could offset the schedule advantage entirely.
